keep: The nomination that won her first Nobel did not have her name on it. A letter from her husband put it there.
lede: The French Academy's nomination for the 1903 prize named her husband and Henri Becquerel. She is on the prize because Pierre answered a letter from Sweden.
copy: Maria Skłodowska came from Russian-ruled Poland to study in Paris, and as Marie Curie did the work two Nobel committees named. The Physics prize of 1903 was for research on the radiation Henri Becquerel had found. The Chemistry prize of 1911 was hers alone, for the discovery of radium and polonium, the isolation of radium and the study of its nature and compounds.

The first prize nearly went without her. Members of the Paris Academy of Sciences, among them Poincaré, Darboux, Lippmann and Mascart, proposed Becquerel and Pierre Curie. Marie was not on it. The Swedish mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler wrote to Pierre to tell him he was being considered. Pierre's reply is dated 6 August 1903. In the American Institute of Physics's translation: 'If it is true that one is seriously thinking about me [for the Nobel Prize], I very much wish to be considered together with Madame Curie with respect to our research on radioactive bodies.' A nomination of her from the year before was found and accepted. The prize was split: half to Becquerel, a quarter each to Pierre and Marie.

Her notebooks are famous for something else. The radioactive particles they absorbed in the laboratory are, says the Bibliothèque nationale de France, still active. The Curie papers came to its manuscripts department in 1967 and were assessed by radiation-protection experts on arrival. They are covered in plastic where needed, and may be consulted only on very particular requests under a strict protocol. Two of them sit in a case in the BnF's museum. A visitor who stands in front of them for ten minutes receives about 2 nanosieverts.

bio.why: A full human portrait, ambition, grief, scandal and genius alike, drawing on her private papers. This house has read the Nobel Foundation's record, the American Institute of Physics's history of her and the BnF's account of the notebooks, not Quinn.

contested: Who saved the 1903 prize for her, and how near a thing it was. The American Institute of Physics calls Mittag-Leffler a member of the nominating committee; the Association Curie et Joliot-Curie says he was not on a Nobel committee at all, and wrote to Pierre unofficially. The Association names the nomination that rescued her: one sent the year before by Charles Bouchard of the Paris Faculty of Medicine, a corresponding member of the Stockholm Academy. Nor was she merely tolerated once in. On 8 September 1903 Mittag-Leffler asked Henri Poincaré whether it would be more just to give the prize to the Curies alone. Poincaré answered on the 12th that sharing it was fairer, since the Curies were more precise and advanced but Becquerel was the initiator. The Mittag-Leffler Institute holds those letters; this house has read them only as the Association quotes them.
